items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds generally have high melting points?

rubric.why: Identifies the strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.description: Oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
rubric.how: Award for identifying both the ions’ opposite charges and their strong attraction.

rubric.why: Explains why high temperatures are needed to melt or boil the compound.
rubric.description: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome the forces holding the ions together.
rubric.how: Award for stating that substantial energy is needed to overcome the attraction or separate the ions.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain positively and negatively charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Define effusion and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines effusion as gas escaping through a very small opening.
rubric.description: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a very small opening.
rubric.how: Award for identifying gas escaping through a tiny opening or small hole.

rubric.why: Provides an example that demonstrates effusion.
rubric.description: Example: gas escaping from a container through a tiny hole.
rubric.how: Award for an example specifically involving gas escaping through a small opening in a container.

modelAnswer: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a very small opening into a region of lower pressure.
Example: gas escaping from a container through a tiny hole.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how pressure and impurities affect it.

rubric.why: Gives the definition of boiling point.
rubric.description: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid’s vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award for relating the liquid’s vapour pressure to atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of external pressure on boiling point.
rubric.description: Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point; decreasing pressure lowers it.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating the direction of the pressure effect.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of a non-volatile impurity.
rubric.description: A dissolved non-volatile impurity raises the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a dissolved non-volatile impurity raises the boiling point.

rubric.why: Relates intermolecular forces to boiling point.
rubric.description: Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces generally have higher boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for linking stronger intermolecular forces with a higher boiling point.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point, while decreasing pressure lowers it.
A dissolved non-volatile impurity raises the boiling point.
A liquid with stronger intermolecular forces generally has a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: Give four characteristics of colloidal solutions.

rubric.why: Identifies the heterogeneous nature of a suspension.
rubric.description: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a suspension is heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Identifies that suspension particles can be seen.
rubric.description: Suspension particles are large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the particles are visible or large enough to be seen.

rubric.why: Identifies the settling of suspended particles.
rubric.description: The particles settle when the suspension is left standing.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the particles settle on standing or when left undisturbed.

rubric.why: Identifies a method for separating suspension particles.
rubric.description: Suspension particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.
rubric.how: Award for stating that filtration can separate the particles.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
The particles settle when the suspension is left standing.
The particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.
